name: Viridine Green
lede: Viridine Green is a pale yellow-green cataloged three separate times, in Ridgway's 1912 atlas, Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary and the ISCC-NBS system, all landing on the same chip our library also calls [[pale-lime]].

sections.title: Cataloged three times over
sections.body: Ridgway's 1912 systematic nomenclature places it on plate VI, hue 33, tone d [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary separately records it, with an earliest use they date to 1899, on plate 17, chip I6 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the same chip as "light yellow green," block 119 [1]. Our library's [[pale-lime]] sits at the identical measured hex; the next-nearest distinct neighbor is [[light-khaki]] [2]. Further out, [[lumiere-green]] and [[light-green-yellow]] sit in the same small cluster [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a match for Viridine Green in only 29 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.1 percent, rarer than 60 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks weakly in the 1800s, only 1.2 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light tone, in half its appearances [3]. The earliest match, from 1605, is a painting by Francesc Ribalta, three centuries before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912 — a look-alike hue in an old photograph, not the name or the pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].
